challenges.title: Four Different User Roles
challenges.problem: Each role required different permissions, authentication flows and dashboard functionality.
challenges.solution: Designed role-based middleware and separated workflows while keeping shared authentication patterns reusable.

challenges.title: Complex Order Lifecycle
challenges.problem: Orders needed to move through multiple states across customer, restaurant and delivery interfaces.
challenges.solution: Defined a controlled order-state workflow and planned real-time event synchronization through Socket.IO.

challenges.title: Relational Database Design
challenges.problem: Restaurants, foods, users, addresses, carts, orders and delivery agents are heavily connected.
challenges.solution: Used PostgreSQL relationships and structured models to keep the data consistent and easier to query.

solutionPoints: Separated route, controller, service and model responsibilities
Used PostgreSQL for relational business data
Used Redux Toolkit for predictable frontend state
Designed APIs around reusable business workflows
Prepared the system for Socket.IO real-time events

title: How I Structure a Production Ready Node.js Backend
excerpt: A practical approach to organizing controllers, services, models, routes and middleware in a scalable Node.js backend.

content.text: When a Node.js project starts growing, putting controllers, database queries and business logic in the same file quickly makes the application difficult to maintain.
A clean backend structure makes features easier to build, debug and scale. Every layer should have a clear responsibility.

content.code:
src/
├── controllers/
├── services/
├── models/
├── routes/
├── middleware/
├── utils/
├── app.js
└── server.js

content.text: This separation keeps controllers small and prevents SQL or complex business logic from leaking into route files.
There is no single perfect folder structure. The important thing is maintaining clear responsibilities and avoiding unnecessary complexity.
